title: Home recognition for MotionEye(OS) with Fritz!Box using fritzconnection (python)
body:
Hi!

Not much to say here as everything is explained in code comments.

This uses fritzconnection that can be found [here](https://github.com/kbr/fritzconnection)

Here is the code:
```
#!/usr/bin/env python
#coding: utf-8

#This script is launched at boot via cron and runs on my server pi
#(Raspberry Pi 3b+) where it switches MotionEyeOS motion
#detection on another pi (Raspberry pi Zero W) depending on if
#given devices are found in the Fritz!Box (WIFI)network.

#Be aware of that this is a beginners work. If you find anything
#that could be improved feel free to tell me.
#I am from germany and therefore my english is not quite good.
#Sorry ;-)

import os
import time
from credentials import * #Import login data stored in separate file
#(could for sure be improved a lot)

motionstatus = "UNSET" #Workaround to only check status of motion
#detection on first cycle (to minimize network traffic of this script)

#create pid file
pid = str(os.getpid())
f = open('/home/pi/fbhomerecognition_pid', 'w') #Change path to fit your needs
f.write(pid)
f.close()

while True:
    try:
        #Read data from Fritz!Box with fritzconnection and check if given MAC addresses stored in credentials.py are online
        home = 0
        online = os.popen ("python3 /home/pi/fritzconnection/fritzconnection/fritzwlan.py -i 192.168.178.1 -u %s -p %s" % (fbuser, fbpass)).read() #Path depends on where you installed fritzconnection. IP needs to be set to Fritz!Box IP. fbuser and fpbass are stored in credentials.py
        for n in maclist:
            result = online.find(n)
            if result != -1:
                home = 1
            else:
                pass

        #Read status of motion detection from MotionEye(OS)
        if motionstatus == "UNSET":
            status = os.popen("curl http://192.168.178.2:7999/1/detection/status").read() #Change IP to where your MotionEye(OS) is running. Port is standard port. "1" is the number of the camera to check. For more information read MotionEye(OS) wiki
            if status.find("PAUSE")  != -1:
                motionstatus = "PAUSE"
            elif status.find("ACTIVE") != -1:
                motionstatus = "ACTIVE"
            else:
                pass
        else:
            pass

        #Switch motion detection to "ACTIVE" if not already active as none of the devices from maclist are online in Fritz!Box WIFI
        if home == 0:
            if motionstatus == "PAUSE":
                os.system ("curl http://192.168.178.2:7999/1/detection/start") #See line 38
                motionstatus = "ACTIVE"
            else:
                pass
        #Switch motion detection to "PAUSE" if not already paused as one or more devices from maclist are online in Fritz!Box WIFI
        elif home == 1:
            if motionstatus == "ACTIVE":
                os.system ("curl http://192.168.178.2:7999/1/detection/pause") #See line 38
                motionstatus = "PAUSE"
            else:
                pass

        #Wait for x seconds before this runs again
        time.sleep(60)
    except:
        exit()
```

Credentials file for login data:
```
#!/usr/bin/python
# coding: utf-8

 #List of MAC addresses that stop motion detection if they are detected online in the home WIFI
maclist = ("00:00:00:00:00:00", "00:00:00:00:00:00", "00:00:00:00:00:00")

#The user you add here needs some configuration in Fritz!Box. For further info see the fritzconnection documentation.
fbuser = "fbuser" #Fritz!Box username
fbpass = "fbpass" #Fritz!Box password
```

Files for download:
[fbhomerecognition.zip](https://github.com/ccrisan/motioneye/files/3680986/fbhomerecognition.zip)

Hope someone finds this helpfull.

Experienced something similar, but could  get the scheduling in`--setup app_setup.py` working using the `at=` and `period=` option to `pn.state.schedule_task(...)` , instead of `cron=`. 

Similar to cron, the `at=` time can be set as the next start of a period, counting from epoch. Cron is more flexible, so this is more a lukewarm cache scheduling, but it works.

@tomascsantos I came across this issue today. I would imagine we feel the issue more directly coming from North American time zones and the issue seems to be only on startup.  I believe there is a bug in when panel seeds the croniter expression.

https://github.com/holoviz/panel/blob/main/panel/io/state.py#L856
I believe the below needs to be written should  replace `dt.datetime.now()` with `dt.datetime.utcnow()` 

```from croniter import croniter
 base = dt.datetime.now() if at is None else at
 diter = croniter(cron, base)
```

@ledwithQ Looks like you have a decent handle on what is wrong, any chance you could contribute a fix?

Note that Python 3.12 has deprecated `dt.datetime.utcnow()`. And the recommended way is `dt.datetime.now(tz=dt.timezone.utc)`

So when we seed croniter this with the default time (the change I'm pursing), we can use any timezone. I could seek to use additional libraries to determine system time for the seed or my preference is to use the `dt.datetime.now(tz=dt.timezone.utc)` and include a comment sharing why UTC is referenced.

title: Purge files based on disk usage
body:
In my use case I would rather ALWAYS record and delete based on file usage rather than time.  Sometimes a motion event just doesn't trigger; or something might happen in a masked area that I normally wouldn't care about but for some reason now do; and I'd like to have the ability to see it.

Unfortunately with my setup; the file sizes just aren't consistent enough to go just by age, and maximize my available storage.  Periods of high activity tend to make files much larger than when there is very little changing in the scene; nighttime footage is typically smaller than daytime, etc.  This means I have to either err on the side of caution and set a timer short enough to never "go over", or risk losing recordings because I've run out of space.

As such my "gift" to the project. 

It's a very quick and dirty bash script.  I don't know JS or Python otherwise I would have tried to integrate it in directly.  As it stands now it could feasibly be attached to an event (eg anytime a new file would be stored) or simply run via cron periodically.

It does require that all cameras record into one parent directory.  Sub dirs are fine eg:
> /opt/camera/channel1, 
> /opt/camera/channel2/YYYY-MM-DD

however this won't work:

> /mnt/camera1
> /opt/camera2

Or at the very least, it will only work on one of the directories.  It would be relatively simple to pass  variables to the script over-riding things however if you wanted it to operate on a per-channel basis.

The script will only do anything once you're **already** using more than your declared amount, and will only bring you down TO that amount (or rather, the first file deleted that brings you under it).  This means it wont stop you from running out of room if you set the limit to your max available storage; you'll want to leave it low enough for buffer space before the next trigger happens.  As it sits, it deletes one file (plus associated .thumb) at a time, checks the space again, and repeats until it gets below that limit.  At the end, if you've emptied a directory; it'll delete that as well.

It would be simple as well to modify and have a "start" and "stop" limit on it.  EG trigger when you've hit 5TB used, delete until there's only 4TB used; you'd just have to add an extra variable and change line 30 to compare $SIZE against that lower limit.

I parse the motioneye.conf file for two variables ("max_size" in MB and "media_path" for the parent directory of the recordings); but I've also set it where you can ignore those and just declare those settings inside the script.

I tried to keep it as generic as possible for cross-platform use but I can't make any promises that it'll work on anything other than my own system :-)


[disk_clean.sh.txt](https://github.com/ccrisan/motioneye/files/1574002/disk_clean.sh.txt)

I've got myself such functionality with quicker & dirtier approach. It just checks if disk usage is greater than 95%, if so removes recordings with hysteresis to 90% of disk usage:

```sh
#!/bin/sh

cd /mnt/6c5c6e37-de46-4411-a55e-46467f4111ed/motioneye
if [ `df -B1 /mnt/6c5c6e37-de46-4411-a55e-46467f4111ed | tr -s ' ' | tr -d % | tail -n 1 | cut -d ' ' -f 5` -ge 95 ] ; then
        while [ `df -B1 /mnt/6c5c6e37-de46-4411-a55e-46467f4111ed | tr -s ' ' | tr -d % | tail -n 1 | cut -d ' ' -f 5` -ge 90 ] ; do
                find -name "*.*" -type f -printf '%T@ %p\n' | sort -k 1nr | sed 's/^[^ ]*//' | tail -n 1 | xargs echo
                find -name "*.*" -type f -printf '%T@ %p\n' | sort -k 1nr | sed 's/^[^ ]*//' | tail -n 1 | xargs rm -f
        done
fi
```

Having any of these solutions somewhat added to motioneye would be cool!
This would be a great feature. I don't know how long it's going to take to fill my SD card, and it's unlikely to match 1 day/week/month anyway.

It's the only thing keeping me on BlueIris.

Supporting this request. I have my disk filling up constantly, so disk space is more important to me than having X months of footage. In my case it would be more useful to limit the size and not the time.

title: vendor libstdc++ and clingo for bootstrapping from source in arcane environments
body:
One alternative to #20068 (possibly complementary?) is to attempt to hack away at the build system for clingo (CMake) so that it will avoid introducing a requirement on a C++14 compiler and we can reliably bootstrap it from source in arcane environments.

<!--*Please add a concise summary of your suggestion here.*-->

### Rationale
Removing the futuristic and unnecessary C++14 requirement doesn't break anything (yet)! It currently doesn't require more than a small patch:
https://github.com/cosmicexplorer/clingo/commit/a1db68ee31fb4a78a3236c94c356cb2b7e803fe8

<!--*Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe it!*-->

### Description

**I found the above clingo commit built and was successfully importable with python 2.6.7, and editing the CMakeLists.txt as in the HEAD commit avoids producing any command lines requiring a C++14 compiler!** 

So *only two changes* are necessary to keep this clingo patchset up to date and buildable on e.g. RHEL/CentOS 7 as per #20069! If we hooked that up into spack, it would likely be a lot more stable / a lot less tech debt than a fork (which I was previously worried about for some version).

<!--*Describe the solution you'd like and the alternatives you have considered.*-->

### Additional information
<!--*Add any other context about the feature request here.*-->

I think #20068 seems **100% orthogonal to this approach** -- rather, developing *a reliable (reproducible?) method of bootstrapping from sources* seems like the key to both of these issues. If we can trust our robust script, we can easily re-ship updated binaries for multiple architectures as in #20068, while ensuring via CI that our bootstrap script avoids correctness (or performance?) regressions as we try to self-bootstrap.
 
I think from any self-bootstrapping process for a tool like spack that runs itself from source, I as a user might (eventually) have these requirements:
1. [ ] Users will clearly understand when a bootstrap occurs (can possibly cancel it if performed as a transaction?).
2. [ ] Users will be able to point spack to their own internal toolchain binary distribution server (servers?) without any configuration.
    - Spack could (like pants does) assume such a server's endpoints are laid out corresponding to a hierarchical filesystem tree.
     - The docs clearly and unambiguously state how to do this.
3. [ ] There is a tag created specifically to track issues with binary resolution.

### General information

**It looks like spack already exposes the entry point for cron jobs/etc to clean up space with [`spack gc`](https://spack.readthedocs.io/en/latest/basic_usage.html?highlight=garbage#garbage-collection), and if we can make the bootstrap "look like a normal spack install", we may be able to get control of that like this for free**.

Relatedly, here's a really interesting discussion thread from the pants repo on invalidating external binaries: https://github.com/pantsbuild/pants/pull/10768#discussion_r487462675
> Aaaaand ... this is still broken in realistic ways. Namely, upgrading or downgrading a binary found here previously will result in the same output from this rule and thus not trigger a re-run of rules depending on this data, which is wrong. The only cases currently covered by this fix from the list below are 1 and 2:
>
>    An applicable binary is added to the search path.
>    An applicable binary is removed from the search path.
>    An applicable binary on the search path is modified (upgraded or downgraded most likely).
>
> To handle 3 the contents of the discovered binaries need to be hashed (And even that is not enough! Dynamically linked libraries could change the binaries output ... but we'll need to whistle past the graveyard - that level of detail can really only be addressed by always running in an image / using a local docker / podman / runc / crun type solution). This could be done by storing it in the CAS as a hack, but we won't / can

Lets also provide each user with a scratch directory that cleans up files more than 30 days old. 

## The Plan (by @yarikoptic and @asmacdo )

- [ ] develop a simple efficient script which would dump listing of content on EFS into a json or jsonlines file (might be worth compressing it right away with built-in to python compressor?)
   - [ ] just run it interactively on an EC2 instance to get idea on the time/size requirement 
   - [ ] add to that script information on date when it ran and how long it took to execute
- [ ] attach that script to be ran by AWS lambda and upload produced listing somewhere
   - [ ] unversioned S3 bucket might be the best choice
- [ ] develop a script which consumes that dump and 
   - [ ] does analysis according to the policy (#188)
   - [ ] eventually manages (sends, marks sent etc) notifications

Sample scripts from chatgpt to collect and analyze stats are available at https://chatgpt.com/share/6732630c-4e54-8002-bf09-41df8175b6d0 .

After chatting with @yarikoptic, we probably should not be too ambitious with a cron job. 

All above should be run only prior to a migration (or kicked off manually if we want to reclaim some space).

There may still be a good use for a cron job-- cleaning up files older than X in a provided scratch dir.

I think we should indeed not cleanup anything automatically, especially since we are not tracking "access time" but only "modification time" on files - we can't make judgement if anything is still in use or not.

What cron job should do is per user:
- check when user last used/logged in to hub
  - since we do not keep that info AFAIK, let's use last dandiarchive login information
  - that datetime would serve us as "cache-recency-identifier"
- if for  a given `cache-recency-identifier` we do not have up-to-date "statistics" for the user
  - run script to `du` entire `home/{user}` and `/shared/{user}`

     - find `_pycache_` and `nwb-cache` folders and pip cache and mtime > 30? days -- total sizes and list of them
  - Given any of below conditions are met, email user to notify about usage (list large outdated files etc) and notify about possible actions to be taken (to be decided), and annotate record that for that recency identified email was sent out
    - Conditions: 
      - total du exceeds some threshold (e.g. 100G)
      - total outdated caches size exceeds some threshold (e.g. 1G)
      - prior notification was sent more than a week ago
    - Actions:
      - ask to login and clean up 
- after a sweep, given a list of users and their  `cache-recency-identifier`s, per each user

body:

code runs, however there is no notification. 

```
return notifier.notify({
  title: 'foo',
  message: randomMessage(),
})
```
Same issue with PM2. So it appears that when it's being ran by some different process, not from user's shell, then it fails to send notification to desktop.

Same issue when using with `gnome-session-properties`. Linked SO question: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49221716/when-using-notify-send-inside-some-process-runner-such-as-cron-or-pm2-notificat

**Versions:**
Ubuntu 16.04 Gnome3 (gubuntu distro).
notify-send 0.7.6
"node-notifier": "^5.2.1",

comments.body: @kunokdev did you end up figuring this out? It seems I'm having the same problem.

@NicolasPerl Unfortunately, I haven't. Spent whole night debugging linux `notify-send` (which is used as shell command within this lib for Linux) and I couldn't fix it. However, I think it's related to users, CRON is one user, Desktop environment is other user, and active shell user is third. So perhaps, desktop environment user has no access to crontab user's actions or vice versa. This needs deeper inspection tho. Also, in some edge cases this code worked, I don't know why and I couldn't debug it because I was doing presentation at that moment (and my bot's notification popped up that time, and never once again or before)
Can confirm this is working: https://github.com/mikaelbr/node-notifier/issues/148

I'm trying to send notifications from cron, and the notifications don't display under ubuntu 19.04.
It does work under task scheduler on windows 10, though (using the exact same scripts).

Trying to run `notify-send` in general from cron does not work properly, but I found a this on SO which makes it work correctly from cron
` * * * * *  XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/$(id -u) notify-send Hey "this is dog!`

So in my .sh script I've added
`export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/$(id -u)` to the top of it, and that has made it work from cron for linux.

My experience with this is, running via pm2, it works out of the box on my Mac, but not on a Win10 machine. (the script run by itself shows the notification on Win10, but not if run via pm2). Still trying to figure it out.

Actually, upon further testing, it appears that my issue on Windows 10 was linked to the way I had pm2 starting up. I used nssm (Non-Sucking Service Manager) to make pm2 startup on Win10. At first I made it startup as a system user, which was the main problem. After I edited the pm2 service with nssm to start as a specific regular user, notifications worked for me. Hoping this can help someone.

## TODO:

- [x] Test with 1M users in CICD. Make sure users are generated in a way that have various login methods, tenancy, metadata, roles etc. Make sure the time the test takes is not too much, and things work well and are consistent.

- [x] Create an API for starting/stopping the cron job, and an other one for getting the status of the cron job (active/inactive). The processing batch size should be a parameter for the starting API.

- [x] Allow developers to configure parallelism in ProcessBulkImportUsers cron job

    Currently, it takes on an average 66 seconds to process 1000 users. This is very slow if we are processing a large number of users. This happens because we loop through the users one by one in a for loop and also use just 1 DB connection for BulkImportProxyStorage.

    The solution is to process users parallely using threads and create a BulkImportProxyStorage instance for each user (that is being processed). The number of users we will process in parallel will depend on the `BULK_MIGRATION_PARALLELISM` config value set by the user. This will be a SaaS protected prop and can be added to `PROTECTED_CONFIGS` in CoreConfig.java. It should have the `@NotConflictingInApp` annotation.

- [ ] PR changes in [supertokens-core PR](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core/pull/966)
      - All the PR changes are done but there maybe more changes after review.
- [ ] PR changes in [supertokens-postgresql-plugin PR](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-postgresql-plugin/pull/211)

- [ ] Changes in [Node Script](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core/pull/977) to add users

  The script needs to re-written to optimise for the following user stories - 

    * The user is not expected to monitor the script. The script should try to continue processing and retry failures wherever possible.

    * The user should be able to re-run the script using the same input file multiple times and the script should process the remaining users. This can be implemented by maintaining a state file per input file name.

    * The Core API calls should have an exponential backoff retries (unlimited) in case we get an error from the Core. This is to ensure that we don't halt processing in case the Core is down for a few seconds.

    * The script should continue showing the Bulk Import Cron Job status after it has added all the users. Any users with status=`FAILED` will be added to the same `usersHavingInvalidSchema.json` file. This file could also be renamed to be something like `usersHavingErrors.json`. Since, we will be writing to the `usersHavingErrors.json` file, they are expected to wait until all the users have been processed and then fix the error file and add those users again.

    * The script should display progress logs while adding the users. This could include total number of usrs, number of users added, number of users having errors, etc.

    * We also need to re-search about the size limit of the JSON file. A JSON file having a million user would be about 880 MB. JSON files cannot be streamed, the whole file needs to be read in memory. If this is an issue then we may need to switch to `ndjson` file format which allows streaming the file.

   * Write the docs for Bulk Import using [this outline](https://github.com/supertokens/supertokens-core/issues/912#issuecomment-2136887644).

- [ ] Update the CDI spec to include `/bulk-import/import` and `

We have been discussing it internally but haven't found any solution yet -- that every pod should be able to discover every pod directly in the same StatefulSet is how Kubernetes works and that is exactly we have designed YugabyteDB to work. Given that there is no global DNS (that can handle such pod-to-pod discovery) across multiple Kubernetes clusters, we had found that our [documented approach](https://docs.yugabyte.com/latest/deploy/kubernetes/multi-cluster/gke/helm-chart/) was the simplest way to get such a global DNS.

comments.body:
This will be tricky to solve because the avmfritz binding uses asynchronous polling and sending requests. In such a setup it may occur that requests overlap a little like in your case.

What currently happens is following flow:

1. polling request is sent to F!Box
2. binding receives an ON/OFF command for the outlet - internal state if the channels changes
3. binding sends command to F!Box
4. polling request returns successfully and overrides the previous channel state with the latest value from F!Box
5. send command returns successfully
6. next polling process starts and finally updates the channel state with the new value

To break such a behavior we eventually have to refactor the binding completely and have to introduce a kind of blocking queue to handle all requests.

Comment only - we observe similar behaviour with Modbus binding, which also polls asynchronously.  An "old" update can arrive just after a command is sent out, but before it takes effect at the device. It's an inherent problem with polling.

A cosmetic improvement is disabling autoupdate on affected Items - this removes the "bounce" of Item state.  It stays at old state until next poll.
In Modbus this is usually acceptable because we're often talking once per second poll rates.

Not so good for fifteen minute cycles, though.
I understand the zwave binding can force an extra read poll kind of action a fixed time after issuing a command, perhaps this is a possible way to go.

comments.body:
Hey @moerkey,

the correct parent _process_ of datadog-ipc-helper would be systemd itself, being pid 1; i.e. that's what happens when a process is daemonized (forks itself twice and kills the first fork).

Systemd thinks the datadog-ipc-helper belongs to php8.0-fpm.service as both share the same cgroup, given that a php-fpm process is starting it.

I'm not sure why systemd puts the datadog-ipc-helper into /system.slice/salt-minion.service for you though, after the original cgroup terminates.

As far as I have researched, it doesn't seem to be possible to put the datadog-ipc-helper into another cgroup (generally) as the fpm and apache processes are running as www-data, but nearly everything needs root and it's not like there's an user session active for www-data either, which could inherit it.

I am not sure what or whether we're able to do about this.

The process can currently be disabled by disabling telemetry, but for example ASM also relies on that telemetry, and in future more things will be sent through it.

Hey @bwoebi, 

thank you for the explanation. At first, I would fix that the process does not run as root (user who installed the app) after an installation or update of Datadog PHP tracer. It should run as www-data right? Currently, I need to reboot the system that it runs as this user.

Out of curiosity. How does the process start itself, or who starts it?
And where is the binary? I could not find it on disk.

Cheers

It does not matter as which user the daemon runs, and can be communicated with by any user over its shared memory unix socket.
It simply is spawned by the first php process, i.e. the first time php with the extension code is executed.

This issue has been marked as stale because it has not had activity in the past half year. It will be closed in 7 days if no further activity occurs. Feel free to reopen it if you are still working on it.

Closing this out — this turns out to be a needrestart-side false positive, not something dd-trace-php itself needs to fix.

needrestart checks the process's /proc/<pid>/exe against $nrconf{blacklist}. Since datadog-ipc-helper's exe resolves to /memfd:spawn_worker_trampoline (as explained by @bwoebi above), it gets flagged as an "obsolete binary".

Workaround — add to /etc/needrestart/needrestart.conf (or a conf.d snippet):

    push @{$nrconf{blacklist}}, qr(^/memfd:spawn_worker_trampoline$);

or more generally (matches upstream needrestart's own default since v3.9):

    push @{$nrconf{blacklist}}, qr(^/memfd:);

Confirmed working on needrestart 3.5 (Ubuntu 22.04) and 3.6 (Ubuntu 24.04). Note that Ubuntu's needrestart packages (jammy/noble, as of writing) don't ship the broader /memfd: blacklist entry that upstream added in 3.9, so this still needs to be added manually on current Ubuntu LTS releases.
I think this was might recently have been fixed by itself, given that we no longer default to memfd, but execute ddtrace.so directly via the dynamic linker now?

> I think this was might recently have been fixed by itself, given that we no longer default to memfd, but execute ddtrace.so directly via the dynamic linker now?

Will check it. Can take a while. Need to wait for Devs to patch the old instances.

Thanks @bwoebi — confirmed on 1.25.1. datadog-ipc-helper is now spawned via the
dynamic linker (#3869, since 1.20.0): /proc/<pid>/exe resolves to
ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 instead of /memfd:spawn_worker_trampoline, and needrestart
no longer reports php-fpm because of it.

For anyone stuck on tracer < 1.20.0 with needrestart < 3.9 (Ubuntu 22.04/24.04):
    push @{$nrconf{blacklist}}, qr(^/memfd:);
in /etc/needrestart/conf.d/*.conf works around it.

comments.body: Thanks for the report, I'll look into this.

Hi @npajkovsky, sorry this sat for so long.

The header folding was rewritten in 1.0.0 and the stray blank lines are gone: line breaks already present in a `Text` value are kept as folds, and new folds only go before existing whitespace.

For your use case (copying headers from a parsed message), `Raw` is the type to use. `Text` is for unstructured values that may need RFC 2047 encoding, and a long `Text` value gets written as encoded-words, which you don't want for a `Received` header. With `Raw` the value from mail-parser goes out as it came in, with the original folding:

```rust
builder.header("Received", Raw::new(value))
```

which on 2.0.0 writes

```
Received: from 139-162-244-188.cprapid.com
	by 139-162-244-188.cprapid.com with LMTP
	id RQb5Ojfdd2O5LikAqCNTnA
	(envelope-from <pajkovsky@139-162-244-188.cprapid.com>)
	for <pajkovsky@139-162-244-188.cprapid.com>; Fri, 18 Nov 2022 19:29:59 +0000
```

I'll close this one, but feel free to reopen if you still see wrong output on 2.0.0.

title: how to auto sync without promting for the password everytime

Is there any way around so it does not asks for pass-keys everytime while syncing through ssh or https?

     "syncSettings.crons": {
         // "review": "0 * * * *",      // every hour
         "download": "0 8 * * *", // at 8AM, every day
         "upload": "0 * * * *" // every hour
     },
```

```yml
profile: flutter 

# sync on remote git
repository:
  type: git
  # url of the remote git repository to sync with, required
  url: git@github.com:niamotullah/vscode_sync.git
  # branch to sync on, optional (set to `master` by default)
  branch: vscode

comments.body:
The extension uses the `git` command of your system. To avoid any prompting, `ssh` need to be able to connect to `git@github.com`.
The command `ssh -Tv git@github.com` will test that out.
If you have the error `git@github.com: Permission denied (publickey).`, you need to have your public key added (with the command `ssh-add`).

title: Automated 'grub-pc' security update failing on some platforms.
body:
**Issue:**

Automatic security update of `grub-pc` package fails.

**Affects:**

All AMI (AWS EC2), OVA & VMDK v16.x appliances released to date. ISO & LXC/Proxmox builds are NOT affected.

**Severity:**

PITA - This issue means that the recent `grub-pc` package update isn't installed (and thus remains vulnerable) on TurnKey v16.x systems. On face value that doesn't sound good. But it's not as bad as it sounds... Of the 7 CVEs patched by the `grub-pc` security update, only [CVE-2021-20233](https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/CVE-2021-20233) appears to be relevant to TurnKey users. And that one relates to USB... (For full details; please see Debian Security Advisory [DSA-4867-1](https://www.debian.org/security/2021/dsa-4867.html)).

----

I will provide further details about the issue below (scroll down to "What the issue looks like"), but first I'll post what to do:

### To resolve - or check if you're ok (simplified)

Log into your server as `root` (or `admin` for AWSMP users). Then manually ensure that there are no broken pacakges:
```
apt install --fix-broken
```
(AWSMP users, will need to pre-fix `sudo`).

If it responds like this:
```
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree       
Reading state information... Done
0 upgraded, 0 newly installed, 0 to remove and 0 not upgraded.
```
Then you are NOT AFFECTED and you can safely ignore the rest of this post.

If you have been hit with this issue, then it will interactively ask you where to install `grub` (the default bootloader). First you should see this screen:

![Screenshot from 2021-03-16 16-56-46](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/818633/111262885-149e1000-8679-11eb-94af-8c844b58b425.png)

As that text notes, there is no harm in installing it places it doesn't need to be. But to ensure that this (and any future grub updates) are installed to the correct place it is important that it is installed to where it needs to be.

As part of the build process, we always install grub to the primary (and only) disk image that contains TurnKey Linux. In the case of OVA/VMDK builds that should be `/dev/sda`; in the case of our AMI (AWS EC2 instance) that should be `/dev/xvda`.

The next screen will ask you to select where to install (OVA/VMDK):

![Screenshot from 2021-03-16 16-58-01](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/818633/111263716-6eeba080-867a-11eb-8424-c560c096cd7a.png)

Assuming that you haven't added any additional volumes, then you only need to install to `/dev/sda` in OVA/VMDK; or `/dev/xvda` AMI (AWS EC2). If you have additional permanent volumes in use on your server, then unless you are 100% sure which is which, please don't hesitate to install to all disks. It's important to note, that if you have ANY DOUBT at all, please install it everywhere you can!

To select the relevant places to install grub, please use the arrow keys to move up & down the list, space to select/deselect the individual options and tab to move between the list and the "Ok". Here's is what OVA users might expect after selecting `/dev/sda`:

![Screenshot from 2021-03-16 16-58-40](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/818633/111264333-6b0c4e00-867b-11eb-8817-6d6d38e935b4.png)

Once you click Ok, it will go about installing grub to the relevant place. Please note that any of the following warnings/errors can _safely be ignored_:

- `File descriptor 3 (pipe:[xxxxxxx]) leaked on vgs invocation. Parent PID xxxxx: grub-install`
- `grub-install: error: unable to identify a filesystem in hostdisk//dev/sda; safety check can't be performed.` (or `hostdisk//dev/xvda` for AWS users).
- `grub-install: warning: File system 'ext2' doesn't support embedding.`
- `grub-install: warning: Embedding is not possible.  GRUB can only be installed in this setup by using blocklists.  However, blocklists are UNRELIABLE and their use is discouraged.`
- `grub-install: error: diskfilter writes are not supported.`
----

### What the

comments.body: @JedMeister status on this bug?

@OnGle - this is still an issue...

The essence is that unless the user installs from ISO, the grub install location is not configured. When grub updates occur, grub does not know where to install to which will cause the error. The workaround is fairly straight forward; pre-seed the grub install location.

E.g. on a AWS EC2 instance:

```
debconf-set-selections <<< "grub-pc grub-pc/install_devices multiselect /dev/xvda"
```

Or for a OVA/VMDK VM:

```
debconf-set-selections <<< "grub-pc grub-pc/install_devices multiselect /dev/sda"
```

To fix/close this issue, this needs to be done within buildtasks.
It seems like grub installer cannot work with symbolic links. After applying recommendation from previous comment - it installed with any issue. Before it was as defined at screenshot below:
I'm going to assume this is resolved and close it. If that's not the case please reopen or open a new issue.

title: [backend] Create an incremental backup script that doesn't freeze SQL
body:
Disclaimer: I love UX and frontend, so my backend / SQL skills are lacking.

Currently I am using a CRON job to make daily backups. I had to set compression level close to the lowest (which is still very good for SQL text).. otherwise the server was killing the thread due to taking too much time.

As of writing, it takes a little over a minute to create a `.tgz` backup of the entire Kanji Koohii database. It is convenient to have a single file. However, the mysqldump + archive **freezes the server for about a minute**.

This is bad for users and just bad for my backups too.

## Solution 1 : simple? But how?

I have to find some kind of incremental backup. I don't know if I can do that with a long command line alone with `mysqldump`? Potentially query all the tables based on last edit timestamp to output only the rows from the last week, for example. This would drastically reduce the time it takes to do a backup as well as the archive size obviously, although it would require careful consideration of the indexes on the tables (so the rows can be selected by timestamp fast).

This could be a simple and satisfying solution **IF** and only if I can just overwrite the last full backup with the incremental ones. Eg. do MySQL `source  incremental-backup.sql` one after the other. Otherwise I would have something complicated to restore in case of emergency as well as duplication for testing locally.

This also assumes I still do a full backup but only once a week for example. 

## Solution 2 : use a custom backup script

So I know forums like MyBB have a "task" system. Well is there a generic solution out there for MySQL backups? It sounds like a problem someone already solved and that doesn't need to be too specific to an app. You'd tell the script what your schema looks like, and it would do the above, based on criteria like how far back to save (eg. last week), the naming of the output SQL files, etc.

Ideally such a script wouldbe able to piece back together a full snapshot of the database from the incremental backups so you don't have to manually piece it back together.

## Specs

I'm afraid the backend uses Symfony 1.x but doesn't use the built-in ORMs for legacy reasons. The website has seen two big refactors in the past 11 years, and it's currently using something very close to the Zend Db API so a solution based on that is best. Although for a backup script just safely built `mysql_xyz` calls is fine too. 

It's not super urgent. Any advice from people with SQL experience very much appreciated. As well as recommendations for php packages I could look into?

comments.body:
It may be possible to get big improvements by tweaking the mysqldump command.

The `--quick` option makes the dump more efficient, but is quite likely enabled already.

With InnoDB, the `--single-transaction` option allows the website to keep working while the backup is in progress, rather than locking the tables.

If the server is still overloaded with these options, it may be possible to slow down the backup, so it takes longer but uses a lower proportion of the resources at any one moment (only for InnoDB single-transaction). `nice` doesn't help with the actual dumping, because the work for that is done by the server process, but it might be useful if too much CPU time is going to compression. This person claims to have reduced the dumping resource use by limiting the bandwidth with `cstream` : http://serverfault.com/a/313232

Thank you @HelenFoster 

> Re: InnoDB

The stories which is several hundred MB was converted to InnoDB, most other tables are MyISAM.

I think the CPU usage is not a concern. But I pipe the mysqldump into gzip and I think that's the part which is slow. The thread gets killed if it takes too long.

Here is what a CRON job looks like:

```bash
mysqldump --opt -u user -ppassword db_name | gzip -v1 - > `/bin/date +\%F`-db_name.sql.gz
```

I used to have `-v9` in there and that would get killed because it takes longer to archive so I switched it to lower compression.

I just realized I could potentially split those in successive CRON jobs so the gzip is done in a second step but I'd rather keep it as simple as I can.

Indeed, the backup is locking the database, so the website can't do anything until the backup is finished.

Your idea of doing the gzip in a second step would reduce the time for which the database is locked.

Does the large InnoDB story table need to be perfectly consistent with the others? I guess the story table has references to the MyISAM tables; if there are no references the other way, and the sort of things the story table refers to don't get deleted, then backing up the story table first might be an option.

Note to self:

- split mysql export to backup the two largest tables (stories and flashcards) on separate days, alternating

title: [Feature] Compress backup files
body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
When using mariadb-dump/mysqldump, you can pipe its output to a compression program, for instance, gzip or 7z, and compress the resulting dump file on a single step.
As far as I know, this is currently not possible with the mariadb-operator `Backup` resource, and if you want to compress the dump you have to do so manually.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add a `spec.compress` field to the `Backup` resource, which can be a boolean, or a string that indicates the compression type (gzip, 7z, zstd, etc.). If compression is enabled, the backup job would compress the file using the selected compression program, and then save it.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
N/A

**Environment details**:
- Kubernetes version: 1.27.5
- Kubernetes distribution: k3s
- mariadb-operator version: 0.24.0
- Install method: Helm
- Install flavor: Recommended

**Additional context**
As for now, what we're doing to save compressed dumps is using the Backup resource to generate a dump, save it to an NFS volume mapped in Kubernetes, and then we have a cron job on the server that reads the file, compresses it using gzip, and uploads it to S3 using the AWS CLI.
Now that there's support for directly uploading dumps to S3 in mariadb-operator (which I've been testing and works well for our use case), it would be very useful to have the option of compressing the dumps before uploading them to S3, so we can eliminate the manual steps.

apiVersion: mariadb.mmontes.io/v1alpha1

  name: backup
